0.0.n: 私 means I; adding の makes it possessive here.

0.1.n: Links 私 to 会社 to show whose company it is.

0.3.n: Marks the company as the setting where this schedule applies.

0.4.n: Added after で to make the workplace setting the topic.

0.5.n: 半 after an hour means thirty minutes past that hour.

0.6.n: Marks 9時半 as the time identified as the start of work.

0.7.n: A noun referring to the beginning of the working day.

1.0.n: Refers to the period before noon, rather than a specific morning hour.

1.1.n: Makes the morning the topic, potentially contrasting it with other parts of the day.

1.2.n: Combines with で to describe doing something without other people.

1.3.n: Marks the way the speaker wants to concentrate: 一人で.

1.4.n: A noun used with をする here; 集中する without を is also common.

1.5.n: Connects 集中 to したい, treating concentration as the activity the speaker wants to do.

1.6.n: する changes to したい to express the speaker’s desire.

1.7.n: Connects the desire to concentrate with the resulting scheduling choice.

1.9.n: 系 attached to 作業 means a type or category, describing practical tasks rather than communication.

1.10.n: Links 作業系 to 仕事 so that it describes the kind of work.

1.11.n: Refers to the tasks the speaker schedules.

1.12.n: Marks 仕事 as what the speaker puts into the schedule.

1.13.n: 入れる becomes polite 入れています; here it describes the speaker’s regular scheduling practice.

2.0.n: 私 refers to the speaker and becomes possessive with the following の.

2.1.n: Links the speaker to their main work.

2.2.n: An English loanword used with の to describe 仕事.

2.3.n: Connects メイン to 仕事, making メイン a description of the work.

2.4.n: Refers to the speaker’s primary professional role.

2.5.n: Marks 私のメインの仕事 as what the speaker is explaining.

2.6.n: An English loan expression naming the speaker’s main responsibility.

2.7.n: The linking form used after a noun before ので; together, なので means because it is.

2.8.n: Introduces a reason whose result continues in the next line.

3.0.n: An English loanword referring to the speaker’s work group.

3.1.n: Links チーム to みんな, identifying which people the speaker means.

3.2.n: Refers to all the people on the team.

3.3.n: Marks the team members as the recipients of the communication.

3.4.n: The name of a workplace messaging service.

3.5.n: Marks Slack as the tool used to communicate.

3.6.n: 連絡する means to contact; this segment joins たり to form 連絡したり.

3.7.n: In 連絡したり, たり presents contacting people as one example rather than a complete list.

3.9.n: Refers to requirements or details defining how a project or product should work.

3.10.n: Marks 仕様 as what the speaker thinks through.

3.11.n: The plain form of the verb, used here to name an example activity before など.

3.12.n: Shows that the named activities are examples, not the entire list.

3.13.n: Links the examples ending in など to 作業.

3.14.n: Collectively labels activities such as contacting teammates and planning specifications.

3.15.n: Marks these tasks as what makes up the main part of the speaker’s work.

3.16.n: Used as a noun here, unlike メインの仕事 in the previous line.

3.17.n: Politely completes the statement identifying these tasks as the main part.

0.lit: At my company, as for it, 9:30 is the start of work.
0.tip: では combines the setting marker で with the topic marker は: as for at my company.

1.lit: As for mornings, because I want to concentrate alone, I put task-oriented work into the schedule.
1.tip: 入れています means regularly scheduling tasks here, not physically putting objects somewhere.

2.lit: Because my main job is project management,
2.tip: After a noun, なので means because it is, and the explanation continues into the next line.

3.lit: Tasks like contacting everyone on the team via Slack and thinking through specifications are the main part.
3.tip: たり and など show that the activities are examples, not a complete list.
